full_judgment:
This second Appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the lower Appellate Court affirming those of the Trial Court. 

 5. Against that decree of the Trial Court, the plaintiffs preferred Other Appeal No. 189 of 1972 in the Court of the District Judge, Chittagong. The Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong dismissed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated July 31, 1973. This Second Appeal is against that decree. 

 6. Mr. Mamtazuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that both the Courts below erred in law in holding that the suit for mere declaration that the kabalas and the deed of gift are false, collusive, without consideration and void is not maintainable without a prayer for cancellation of these instruments. He further submits that the lower Appellate Court erroneously dismissed the appeal on the basis of the decision in the case of Daibakilal Basak Vs. Iqbal Ahmed Quarishi and another, 17 DLR 119, Mr. Mamtazuddin submits that the suit as framed for simple declaration is maintainable, the kabala and the deed of gift ab initio void for want of passing of any consideration and the plaintiff being in possession there is no necessity for a decree for cancellation of the deeds and mere declaration is sufficient. 

 7. Mr. Moqbul Ahmed, appearing for the respondents submits that the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for cancellation of deeds as the suit falls within the mischief of section 39 of Specific Relief Act. Placing reliance upon the decision in the case of Daibakilal Basak he submits that where in a suit although the plaintiff is not a party to the document and claims title under the person who created the document he must pray for cancellation of the documents and mere declaration that the documents is void and not binding on him is not sufficient. The relevant provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is that where any person is entitled to any right as to any property he may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny his title to such right and the court may in its discretion declare that he is screntitled and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief. Proviso to section 42 provides that no court shall make an such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so. Section 39 of the Act provides that any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left standing, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled and if the instrument is registered the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the Officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation. Thus from reading both the sections it seems to me that in either case it is the discretion of the Court to decree the suit or not. But section 39 of the Act not only relates to declaration but it also relates to cancellation of the instrument. The learned Judges of the Full Bench of the Dhaka High Court in the case of Daibakilal Basak which was relied on by both Mr. Mamtazuddin Ahmed and Mr. Moqbul Ahmed had occasion to consider a large number of cases and the three learned Judges delivered separate judgments. In that case, the plaintiff asserted his possession in the suit premises through tenants and sought for declaration that the documents are void ab initio and the documents were brought about by the forgeries and false personation for which no consideration passed under the said documents. The Trial Court did not dismiss the suit on the ground of maintainability but the Court directed the plaintiff to pay ad valorem Court fee holding that the plaintiff should pray for a consequential relief by way of cancellation of the document. Against that order the plaintiff obtained a rule and a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court in view of the conflicting decisions on the point of payment of Court fee referred the matter to the Full Bench. Mr. Justice Hasan expressed his view that even if it is accepted that the suit falls within the purview of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, still the plaintiff has got the liberty to seek relief in his own way and the court cannot compel the plaintiff for calling every declaration by way of cancellation of the document which is superfluous. But Mr. Justice Sattar took a contrary view that when a suit falls within section 39, the Court may grant relief by way of cancellation whether it is prayed for or not and the plaintiff is to pay ad valorem Court fees for cancelling the instrument. In considering the plaint mooted before me I feel it profitable to quote the relevant portion of the decision which is necessary for disposal of this appeal. Sayem, J (as his Lordship was then) agreed with the view of Hasan, J and observed relying upon the decision of the Full Bench of Madras High Court in the case of CR Ramaswami Ayyangar Vs. CS Rangachariar & others, 1940 Mad. 113, Harwant Singh Vs. Jagan Nath, 1943 (Lah) 348. Ponnammal Vs. Kanthammal, 1952 Mad. 552 and the case of Rambhorosa Vs. Bina Devi, 1956 Pat. 203. 

 10. For the aforesaid discussions, the judgments and decrees of both the courts below are set aside. I send back the suit to the Trial Court for fresh hearing in accordance with the law.
